articles.title: PNB eyeing bond issuance
articles.description: PHILIPPINE National Bank (PNB) is considering a bond issuance next year to support potential loan expansion, although the timing, size and currency of the offering have yet to be determined. PNB President and CEO Edwin Bautista said the bank had no immediate funding requirement for the rest of the year, as existing deposits remained sufficient to support loan growth. “We can still grow it enough. Our deposits are enough to fund the loan growth,” he told reporters. Bautista said the bank could issue either peso- or US dollar-denominated bonds, depending on the size of the offering and market conditions. Larger issuances would tend to be directed toward overseas markets, where, he said, PNB had received favorable investor interest. The bank prefers longer-term funding, but the timing will depend partly on interest rate movements. Bautista said no issuance had been scheduled for next year and stressed that the bank was not under pressure to raise funds immediately. “Actually, we need it longer,” he said, referring to the tenor of any proposed issuance, noting that prevailing interest rates also remained a consideration. PNB also has room under its existing sustainability bond program, including in the US dollar market, Bautista said. The bank’s funding plans come as it continues to expand its loan portfolio. Bautista said loan growth stood at about 15 percent, below the bank’s internal target but still among the highest growth rates in the industry. “Our loan growth came out about 15 percent. And my budget there is higher than 15 percent,” he said. For the first quarter of 2026, PNB reported loan growth of 15 percent year on year and the pace settled at 10 percent for the first half to P764 billion. The bank’s net income for the first six months stood at P14.6 billion, up 17 percent from a year earlier. Bautista expects loan growth for the full year to remain in double-digit territory, supported by its business-focused loan portfolio and strong deposit base. He said PNB’s capital-to-deposit ratio was approaching 20 percent, indicating that the bank had substantial capital relative to its deposit base. He explained that expanding the balance sheet would require the bank to deploy capital and secure funding to support additional lending. “Normally, what banks do, it’s going to be a mix, right? They go to the capital, to the bond market partly, and partly through better time deposit rates,” he said. On interest rates, Bautista said market rates had largely priced in the possibility of another Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) rate hike in October. He said the size of any adjustment remained uncertain, with a 25-basis-point increase among one of the possibilities. He added that rate increases implemented earlier in the year had already been absorbed into the bank’s lending rates, while the potential impact of another adjustment remained a consideration. On asset quality, Bautista said PNB’s nonperforming loan (NPL) ratio had improved from about 6 percent three years ago and could move closer to the industry average this year. For the first six months of the year, PNB’s gross NPL ratio stood at 4.2 percent, down from 5.5 percent a year ago. Bautista cautioned against treating a high NPL coverage ratio as an automatic indicator of stronger asset quality, saying it could reflect provisions for loans that were already past due but had not yet been classified as nonperforming. Consumer lending accounts for about 8 percent of PNB’s total loan book, with the remaining 92 percent consisting of other lending segments, Bautista said. A big portion of the consumer portfolio is secured, including mortgage loans, while credit cards account for a relatively small share. The bank had sought to expand consumer lending because of its contribution to net interest margins, but Bautista said it was now deliberately slowing credit card expansion amid signs of increasing pressure in the consumer lending market. He said PNB’s longer-term goal of increasing consumer loans to 15 percent of its portfolio would depend on market conditions and borrowers’ capacity to repay, rather than a fixed deadline. The bank’s shares on Friday closed at P76.20, up by P2.40, or 3.25 percent.

articles.title: Indian city resists Google data center
articles.description: BENGALARU, India — Construction of a massive Google data center in the Indian city of Visakhapatnam has been met with resistance from residents who fear the impact on the environment and their lives. But the tech giant says its “gigawatt-scale” artificial intelligence (AI) facility in southern Andhra Pradesh state — part of a $15- billion investment — will use air cooling systems, and not water from an area already facing shortages. Alexander Smith, Google’s head of infrastructure and energy for the Asia-Pacific region, answered Agence France-Presse’s (AFP) questions about the project. Smith said Google takes questions raised by the public seriously. “Independent environmental assessments — covering grid stability, power supply, water risk, ecology, acoustics, and more — are conducted 12 to 24 months before a project begins,” he said. “If there is insufficient power in a location, or if operating a data center would mean taking power away from a community, Google will either find ways to develop more power, or it will not build there,” he added. The data center — Google’s biggest “AI hub” outside the United States — is set to become operational in 2028. It is one of several huge new tech sites planned in Visakhapatnam, but activists are demanding a moratorium on new data centers across Andhra Pradesh until there is more evidence of their impact on the environment and local community. Smith called the project “a multi-decade commitment” that carries “an obligation to be a good neighbor.” “That means the watershed, the grid and the communities around our facilities must be better off for our being here,” he added. Water and power needs As AI use accelerates, construction of power-hungry data centers is booming worldwide, especially in Asia. Critics say they will add demand to electricity grids still heavily reliant on planet-warming fossil fuels, and place new pressure on often-stretched local water supplies to cool down hot servers. Google’s water assessment for Visakhapatnam “pointed to pressure on the local watershed,” Smith said. “That finding shaped our choice of cooling configuration from the outset,” with “advanced air cooling” chosen instead of water cooling. “For the freshwater consumed by non-cooling facility needs, Google is committed to replenishing 120 percent of the volume we consume across our operations by 2030,” he added. Google does not disclose site-level capacity figures for power. But the US giant “fully funds the cost of required power infrastructure upgrades.” “We are planning to invest in new clean energy projects — built above and beyond what regulations require — in Visakhapatnam,” Smith said. Why Google chose Visakhapatnam A Finnish authority recently ordered work to halt on two Google data center sites pending mandatory environmental assessments, and worried residents have also mounted protests in Visakhapatnam. To select global sites, Google looks for “proximity to customers and users, access to talent, potential for new clean energy and opportunities to establish mutually beneficial partnerships with local communities,” Smith said. “Visakhapatnam is one of the few places where all of these come together,” he added. The city’s coastline also allows undersea cables to link Visakhapatnam to South Africa and Australia, “positioning Andhra Pradesh as India’s third major subsea hub,” Smith said. The promised jobs Data center opponents say the benefits of the vast warehouse-like sites rarely trickle down to local residents. Smith said that “a development of this kind is projected to generate approximately $688 million in local economic activity every year.” “For every job inside a Google data center we support nine additional jobs in the surrounding community,” he added. “Over a typical three-to-five-year construction period, an average Google data center development employs about 4,200 construction workers annually,” Smith said. “Each facility is designed to operate for at least 20 years, and once live it sustains hundreds of specialist on-site roles,” he added.

articles.title: World Bank talking with countries on crisis aid
articles.description: BANGKOK — The World Bank is in discussions with 30 to 40 countries about potential crisis aid to help them manage energy shocks and price increases triggered by the war in the Middle East, its president, Ajay Banga, told Reuters in an interview. Banga said the global economy had proven fairly resilient, in part due to big AI investments and adjustments in supply and demand for oil, which meant that few countries had sought the initial $25 billion in crisis funds that the World Bank had made available when the war began in late February. However, a sharp spike in diesel and fertilizer prices and other factors, including the looming super El Niño weather effect, were adding to challenges facing developing countries, Banga said in an interview ahead of this week’s annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank. “There is pressure, and so I think maybe over the coming months, more countries will come for some slice of that first $50 to $60 billion,” Banga said, referring to the initial $25 billion plus another $35 billion that countries could tap by diverting resources from already approved World Bank projects. “We’ll see, but we’re ready. We’re engaged. We’re having conversations with a number of them, you know, 30 to 40 countries are in dialogue with us,” he said. Many developing countries have been hit hard by the spike in energy prices and high interest rates that have increased borrowing costs at a time when their fiscal coffers are still depleted by measures taken during the Covid-19 pandemic and the spike in inflation following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. World Bank estimates show that developing countries owe external creditors about $400 billion in 2026, with interest payments alone comprising one-third of the total. Banga said more countries had shown interest in retooling existing projects than in tapping the immediate crisis window to address their liquidity needs. If the situation worsened, the Bank could make available as much as $100 billion in funds, he said, exceeding the $70 billion disbursed during the pandemic. The World Bank last month announced that it attracted a record $112 billion in private capital in the year ended June versus $69 billion a year earlier, and more than triple the 2022 total before Banga, a former Mastercard CEO, became president. That was on top of the $123 billion invested from the bank’s own resources for that year, for a combined $235 billion, Banga said, underscoring the importance of tapping all available resources, especially at a time when Western countries have sharply cut official bilateral development aid. “There is no one answer that fits when the world has these kinds of issues. What you need to do is figure out how to cut your coat to suit your cloth,” Banga said. Banga said he expected further gains in private capital flows in coming years, aided by expanded political risk guarantees from the bank’s Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency, growth in local currency financing, and continued work on regulatory reforms that made it easier for foreign investors. The private capital jump was biggest in projects in upper-middle-income countries like Argentina or India, which accounted for $50 billion of the private capital, and lower-middle-income countries including Bangladesh and Angola, which accounted for $37 billion. But more work was needed to boost the roughly $3 billion in private capital flowing to low-income countries. “In the smaller countries, it hasn’t multiplied enough, and there are challenges,” he said, noting the bank would announce some new initiatives this week aimed at ensuring micro-, small- and medium-sized businesses also had access to private capital. Banga said private capital growth was also regionally spread, with the largest increase seen in Latin America and the Caribbean, which accounted for $36.3 billion of last year’s total, followed by Europe and Central Asia with $21.3 billion, South Asia with $19.2 billion and Africa with $22 billion. The top 10 recipient countries were Brazil, India, Turkey, Romania, Nigeria, Argentina, South Africa, Bangladesh, Mexico and Chile, the Bank said. Banga said the World Bank and IMF were working together to address the high debt levels plaguing many developing countries through a series of initiatives, including efforts to boost countries’ domestic revenue collections. The Bank had already set up some debt-for-development swaps for Angola and Ivory Coast, and a portfolio-based guarantee for Argentina, and was working on over a dozen more projects. “We’ve got 14 or 15 in the pipeline, helping them rotate out higher-priced old debt for newer-priced debt with our guarantees,” with the difference then targeted at education, healthcare, water, or nature programs, he said. REUTERS
